column4: Consultant: Hi Yvette. Can you hear me all right?
Yvette Carnahan: I can hear you. Hang on, let me shut my door. Okay. Hi.
Consultant: No rush at all. How's your week going so far?
Yvette Carnahan: [laughs] It's Tuesday. Ask me Friday.
Consultant: That bad?

Yvette Carnahan: No, it's a normal week. It's just that a normal week here is a lot of week. Tansy's finishing up with a property manager, she'll hop on in a second, and Curtis said he'd be here. Curtis is our IT guy. Well, he's our IT everything.
Consultant: Good, I'd like to hear from all three of you. Whereabouts are you sitting today?
Yvette Carnahan: Chattanooga. That's our main office. We've got a branch in Knoxville and one in Roanoke.
Consultant: And how many people all in?
Yvette Carnahan: About a hundred and forty. Most of that's field. Ninety-some technicians, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, a bit of general handyman work. Then supervisors, then the office.
Consultant: And your team inside that?
Yvette Carnahan: Client services. Nine people, including Tansy. They're the ones who pick up the phone when a building's got a problem.
Tansy Whitlock: Sorry, can you hear me? My headset's being weird.
Tansy Whitlock: Sorry, can you hear me? My headset's being weird.
Consultant: You're coming through fine now.
Tansy Whitlock: Okay, good. Sorry. That was Marley at the Ridgeline property. She's lovely but she talks.
Consultant: Hi Tansy. I was just getting the shape of the company. Curtis, are you with us?
Curtis Vandergrift: I'm here. I'm on my phone for a minute, I'll be at my desk in five.
Consultant: That's fine. So before I ask you about problems, I want to understand how the work actually moves today. Somebody in a building has a problem. Walk me through what happens.

Tansy Whitlock: Okay. So it comes in one of three ways. Either they call us, which is still most of it, or they email the service inbox, or for two of our clients they put it into their own system and we have to go and find it.
Consultant: Their own system?

Tansy Whitlock: Brightmoor uses ServiceChannel. So their property managers don't call us. They put a work order into ServiceChannel and we're supposed to accept it in there, and then update it in there, and close it in there. And Fairlane, the hospital group, they've got their own maintenance system and we log into that one.
Consultant: So your people are in several places at once.
Tansy Whitlock: Three or four places, all morning.
Consultant: And when it comes in by phone, what happens then?

Tansy Whitlock: Then we open a work order. There's a shared Excel file on the SharePoint with a tab for each month, and we put in the client, the building, what's wrong, who we dispatched it to, the date.
Consultant: You said work order. Is that the same thing as the request that came in, or is it a separate record?
Tansy Whitlock: Same thing, mostly. The request is the phone call. The work order is what we open. Some people say request, some people say WO. It's the same thing to us.
Consultant: Then I'll say work order. And once one is open, how does it get to a technician?

Tansy Whitlock: Depends on the trade and the branch. There's a whiteboard in the dispatch room, techs down the side, days across the top, and whoever's dispatching moves magnets around. Then we text the tech. Or call him, if it's an emergency.
Consultant: So the whiteboard is the real schedule.
Tansy Whitlock: The whiteboard is the truth. The spreadsheet is what we tell people.
Tansy Whitlock: [laughs] That's a good line. Does anything connect the two?
Tansy Whitlock: A person. Me, usually.
Consultant: And Roanoke and Knoxville do it the same way?

Tansy Whitlock: Knoxville's the same. Roanoke came in through an acquisition and they've got their own spreadsheet and their own way of doing it, and their own whiteboard, and honestly I can't see any of it from here.
Consultant: How much work is going through that in a week?
Tansy Whitlock: Reactive, so calls, four hundred-ish a week across the three branches. More in the summer when the air conditioning starts going.
Yvette Carnahan: That's not counting PMs.
Consultant: PMs meaning?

Yvette Carnahan: Preventive maintenance. Every contract has a schedule in it. So many filter changes, so many inspections, quarterly this, annual that. Those are planned months ahead. That's a different animal from a call.
Consultant: Understood, and I'll come back to those, because they sound like a different kind of work. Are the PMs in the same spreadsheet?
Yvette Carnahan: No. They live in Sage. Sort of. They live in Sage and then they live in another spreadsheet that Delia keeps, because Sage won't show them the way we need to see them.
Consultant: Sage being?
Yvette Carnahan: Sage 300. Accounting and job costing. Invoicing comes out of there, and the contract values sit in there.
Consultant: And roughly how much of your contract value is PM work versus reactive?
Yvette Carnahan: About half and half. The PM side is the part that renews, though. That's what a contract is.

Consultant: Good to know. So, work orders in Excel, the schedule on a whiteboard, PMs in Sage and a spreadsheet, two clients' own portals, and Roanoke doing its own thing. What do the technicians carry?
Tansy Whitlock: Phones. They text us photos and they text us done. Some of them fill out a paper ticket and it comes back in the truck on Friday.
Consultant: And that's how you know a job is finished?
Tansy Whitlock: That's how we know if we're lucky.
Consultant: What happens after six o'clock?
Tansy Whitlock: After six it goes to an answering service, and they email the service inbox. So an emergency at seven at night is an email nobody's looking at.
Curtis Vandergrift: Okay, I'm at my desk.

Consultant: Welcome. Curtis, I want your view on the systems side shortly. One more on the current state first. Yvette, where does monday.com come into this? I understood you've got an account already.
Curtis Vandergrift: We do. We tried monday two years ago and it didn't stick.
Consultant: Tell me more about that. What did you try to do with it?
Curtis Vandergrift: I built a work order tracker. Columns for the client, the building, status, who's assigned, a date. It was fine. Nobody used it after about six weeks.
Consultant: Why do you think that was?

Curtis Vandergrift: Honestly? Because nothing came into it by itself. Somebody still had to type the work order in, and they were already typing it into the spreadsheet, so now it's two places. So they did the spreadsheet, because that's what the dispatcher looks at.
Consultant: Did anyone ask the help desk what they needed before it got built?
Curtis Vandergrift: [laughs] No. That was me on a Saturday.
Tansy Whitlock: I didn't know it existed for about a month.
Consultant: That's useful, and I'd rather hear it now than in three months. Is the account still there?
Curtis Vandergrift: Yeah, we still pay for it. Safety uses it, Rob's got an inspections board he likes. And estimating keeps a bid board in there. Fifteen, twenty people in it maybe.
Consultant: Do you know which plan you're on?
Curtis Vandergrift: Standard, I think? Whatever the middle one is. I'd have to look.
Consultant: That's fine, and I'd check it properly before I designed anything, because what's possible depends on it. Is the old work order board still in there?
Curtis Vandergrift: Probably. I haven't opened it in a year and a half. It'll be full of dead work orders from back then.
Consultant: Thank you. That's the picture I needed. So tell me about the problem. If you had to name the thing that made you get in touch, what is it?
Yvette Carnahan: We are missing response times. And it has already cost us.
Consultant: Say more about that.

Yvette Carnahan: Every contract we sign has service levels in it. Emergency is four hours for most clients, two hours for Fairlane because it's a hospital. Urgent is same day or next business day depending on the contract. Routine is five business days. And we're supposed to report on all of it.
Consultant: And what's actually happening?
Yvette Carnahan: We don't know whether we're hitting it until somebody tells us we didn't. Usually the client tells us.
Consultant: When did that last happen?

Yvette Carnahan: The one that hurt was July. Brightmoor, the Carrolton building. A chiller went down on a Friday afternoon. It came into the service inbox at four-something on the Friday and nobody opened that inbox again until Monday morning.
Consultant: What happened?

Yvette Carnahan: Two floors of offices with no cooling, in July, all weekend. Their property manager called my cell phone on the Monday at seven in the morning. That was a four-hour emergency and we responded in about sixty-six hours.
Consultant: And what did that lead to?

Yvette Carnahan: It led to a quarterly review where their director of operations had a slide with our response times on it. Not our numbers. Theirs, out of ServiceChannel. And then a letter putting us on a ninety-day performance plan. That's a formal thing. It goes in the file.
Consultant: What about the contract itself?
Yvette Carnahan: It renews in January. They've told us they'll make the decision on the back of the next two quarterly reviews. The next one is the second week of December.
Consultant: How big is Brightmoor for you?
Yvette Carnahan: Forty-one buildings. It's just under a fifth of our book. I'd rather not put the dollar number on it on a first call.
Consultant: That's fair, and I don't need it today. Was the chiller an isolated thing?
Tansy Whitlock: It's not isolated. It's the weekends and the evenings and the handoffs. Things sit.
Consultant: Where do they sit?

Tansy Whitlock: The inbox. It's a shared mailbox, so everybody can see it and nobody owns it. You open it and there's forty emails, and some of them are work orders and some of them are Marley saying thank you, and you can't tell which ones somebody already dealt with unless they remembered to flag it.
Consultant: How do you get around that today?

Tansy Whitlock: We flag them. Or we drag them into a folder. I've got a rule that drops the Fairlane ones into their own folder. And I do a sweep at the end of my day and anything that looks stuck goes on a sticky note on my monitor.
Consultant: And what stops you carrying on like that?
Tansy Whitlock: It works when I'm here. It doesn't work when I'm on vacation, it doesn't work at five past five, and it really doesn't work on a Friday at four-something.

Yvette Carnahan: And we have already lost a client over it. Not Brightmoor. Cavender Medical, back in March. Six clinics. Their facilities guy said, and I've not forgotten it, he said I never know if you've got it. He wasn't even angry about the work. Our technicians are good. He just couldn't see anything.
Consultant: Who else ends up dealing with this?
Yvette Carnahan: Me. The supervisors, because I'm the one calling them. And the branch managers when I can't get hold of a supervisor.
Tansy Whitlock: And the technicians get it, because they turn up at something that's been sitting three days and the client's already furious with them before they're out of the van.
Consultant: Say nothing changes. Where is this in a year?

Yvette Carnahan: In a year? If we lose Brightmoor in January then we're not growing, we're shrinking, and I'd be looking hard at whether I need nine people in client services. And the contracts we're bidding on now are bigger, and the bigger they are the more reporting they want. So it gets worse, not better, because the work we're chasing has more of this in it.
Consultant: Let's stay with the reporting, because you've mentioned it twice. How does a client get their numbers today?
Tansy Whitlock: I build it. Every month. I pull the spreadsheet, filter it to that client, and go line by line working out whether we made the window.
Consultant: How do you work out whether you made it?

Tansy Whitlock: The date it came in and the date the technician closed it. Except the date it was closed is the date I typed it in, which might be two days after he actually did it. So I know it's not right. I have to go and ask people.
Consultant: How long does that take you?
Tansy Whitlock: Two days. Give or take. Two days out of my month. And then Yvette reads it and finds something that doesn't look right and I do parts of it again.
Yvette Carnahan: Because I can't take it into a quarterly review if I don't believe it. And last time I didn't believe it, and I was right not to.
Consultant: What happened?

Yvette Carnahan: We had ninety-four percent on our sheet and they had seventy-eight on theirs. And I couldn't defend either number in the room. That's worse than being wrong. I sat there with nothing to say.
Consultant: How much of your own time goes into that cycle?
Yvette Carnahan: Half a day a month, more with the follow-up. I'm not going to put a number on my own time.
Consultant: That's fine. Tansy, does anybody else touch the report?
Tansy Whitlock: Delia pulls the PM completion part out of Sage, because that's in the report too. That's another half day of hers.
Consultant: So between the three of you, that's two days, half a day and half a day. Call it twenty-four hours a month?
Tansy Whitlock: Call it twenty. My two days isn't always two days.
Consultant: Twenty it is. And if nothing changes on the reporting side?
Tansy Whitlock: I mean, it just, it's the same every month. It's not getting worse exactly. It's just always there.
Consultant: Understood. You've both mentioned calling supervisors. Tell me what escalation looks like.
Yvette Carnahan: There isn't one, really. There's me calling Dewey.

Tansy Whitlock: Officially, if a work order is going to blow its window, or the technician can't get in, or it needs a part we haven't got, we escalate it to the field supervisor for that trade in that region.
Consultant: And how do you do that?
Tansy Whitlock: Call or text. Usually text.
Consultant: And then what?
Tansy Whitlock: And then nothing, sometimes. You text Dewey and you don't know if he's read it, and he's up on a roof, so fair enough, but I've got a client on hold.
Yvette Carnahan: Dewey is excellent, and Dewey does not answer his phone. Both of those are true.
Consultant: How often does one of those go quiet?
Tansy Whitlock: Every day there's one or two. Out of, I don't know, fifteen or twenty escalations a day across the branches, a couple of them just vanish, and then somebody remembers at four o'clock.
Consultant: What do you do to stop them vanishing?
Tansy Whitlock: I keep a list on a legal pad and I re-text people. That's the system. It's a legal pad.
Consultant: Who else feels that one?
Yvette Carnahan: The client feels it first. Then me, because they ring me. And the supervisors will tell you they're getting texted about the same job by three different people, which is also true.
Consultant: Can you put any cost on the chasing?
Tansy Whitlock: An hour a day each, easily, for the people who aren't stuck on the portals. Just chasing and re-asking.
Consultant: I'll come back to that. You said two of your people are in client portals most of the morning. Tell me about that.

Tansy Whitlock: Brightmoor and Fairlane. Everything they send us we have to accept in their system, then when it's done we close it in their system with a note, and photos sometimes. And we still have to have it in our spreadsheet, because the dispatcher hasn't got a ServiceChannel login.
Consultant: So the same work order gets typed twice.
Tansy Whitlock: Twice, or three times. And their system logs you out every twenty minutes.
Consultant: How long is that, per person, per day?

Tansy Whitlock: Rosalie is in Brightmoor's portal from eight until half eleven, twelve. Every day. Junie does Fairlane, which is a smaller account, but she's got the badging to deal with as well, so call it the same. Three hours each. Easily three hours each.
Consultant: Could that be automated from your side?
Curtis Vandergrift: I looked at it. ServiceChannel has an API, I'm fairly sure, but it's their tenant, not ours, and Brightmoor's IT people were not enthusiastic. I never got past the first email.
Consultant: Understood. So what do you do about it today?
Tansy Whitlock: We type it twice. That's what we do about it.
Consultant: And is that sustainable?
Tansy Whitlock: I mean, it's the job. Rosalie hates it. The girl before Rosalie quit, and she said the portal was part of why.
Yvette Carnahan: I'd add that the portal work isn't optional. It's in the contract. If we don't close it in their system, we don't get paid.
Consultant: That's important, thank you. You mentioned badging.

Tansy Whitlock: Fairlane, you can't just walk in. Everybody's badged, and there are areas where you need an escort. And we're not supposed to put anything about patients or which room in the work order notes. Their compliance person was very clear with us about that.
Consultant: Good, I'll hold on to that. Anything similar anywhere else?
Yvette Carnahan: The contract terms themselves are confidential, all of them. Rates, penalties, all of that. That's between us and the client.
Consultant: Noted. And do you use outside vendors at all?

Yvette Carnahan: We sub out some things. Fire alarm testing, elevators, some roofing. So there are outside vendors who need to know what we need from them and when, and right now that's email as well.
Consultant: Thank you. One more area, then I want to try and put a cost on some of this. When a new person joins your team, how do they learn the job?
Tansy Whitlock: They sit next to me.
Consultant: For how long?
Tansy Whitlock: Realistically? Four months before I'd leave them on their own with Brightmoor.
Consultant: And where's the written version of what you know?
Tansy Whitlock: There's a binder. And there's a folder on the SharePoint with some Word documents in it, and I don't think anybody's opened that since Corinne made it.
Consultant: What sort of thing is in the binder?

Tansy Whitlock: Who to call at each building. Which buildings need badges. The after-hours numbers. Which clients you're allowed to quote a price to and which ones you're not. Fairlane has a whole page about where you're allowed to park.
Consultant: How often does somebody have to come and ask you something that's already in there?
Tansy Whitlock: All the time. I couldn't tell you a specific one, it's just the day.
Consultant: Is that a couple of times a week, or more than that?
Tansy Whitlock: More than that. I don't want to guess at it.

Consultant: That's fine. I'd rather have nothing than a made-up number. Let me try and put a rough cost on the part we do have numbers for, and I want your numbers, not mine. Tansy, you said three hours each for Rosalie and Junie on the portals.
Tansy Whitlock: Three each, five days a week.
Consultant: That's thirty hours a week between them. And you said an hour a day each for chasing, for the people who aren't on the portals. How many people is that?
Tansy Whitlock: Seven, with me.
Consultant: So thirty-five hours a week there. Sixty-five hours a week altogether on re-typing and chasing. Does that sound right or wrong to you?
Tansy Whitlock: That sounds about right. It might be light, because that doesn't count the sweep at the end of the day.
Consultant: What does an hour of that time cost the business, loaded, with everything in it?
Yvette Carnahan: Thirty-five? I'd guess thirty-five all in. Don't hold me to that, Pete would know.
Consultant: Pete being?
Yvette Carnahan: Pete Odugbemi, our CFO. He does all the loaded rate work for bids.

Consultant: So if it were thirty-five, then sixty-five hours a week is two thousand two hundred and seventy-five a week, and across fifty-two weeks that's about a hundred and eighteen thousand a year.

Consultant: The reporting is on top of that, and I'm going to leave the money off the reporting, because you've said you don't want to price your own time. That's twenty hours a month, so two hundred and forty hours a year at your number.

Yvette Carnahan: And that's the bit I want to push back on. Not the hours. The hours sound right, if anything they're light. But thirty-five is me guessing, and I don't want a wrong number walking around in front of Pete. Let me get the real one from him, and then we can talk about what it adds up to.

Consultant: That's the right instinct, and I'd rather use his number than mine. I'll hold it as your hours with his rate to come. Two things I'm leaving out of it either way, unless you want to put a figure on them: Cavender, and anything to do with the Brightmoor renewal.
Yvette Carnahan: No. Cavender was six clinics, that's all I'll say. And Brightmoor I'm not discussing until I've talked to Pete.
Consultant: Understood. Different question, then. If those sixty-five hours came back, what would you do with them?
Yvette Carnahan: Rosalie and Junie would be doing account work. Actual relationships with the property managers instead of data entry. And I'd stop being the escalation path.
Consultant: Is there something you'd go after that you can't go after today?

Yvette Carnahan: Yes. There's a county contract going out in the spring. Eleven buildings, and we've seen the draft RFP, and it asks for monthly response-time reporting per building. We can't answer that today. We'd be promising something we can't prove.
Consultant: Do you know what that one's worth?
Yvette Carnahan: Not yet. It'll be a real number. I'm not going to invent one for you.
Consultant: Fair enough. Let's talk about what good looks like. Say this is running well in the spring. What's different in a normal week?

Yvette Carnahan: Every work order is in one place, with a clock on it and a name on it. I can look at one screen on a Monday morning and see what's about to breach and who's holding it. And when I walk into a quarterly review, the numbers on my slide came out of the system, and I can click into any line of it while they're watching.
Tansy Whitlock: And I'd like to not be the system. I'd like to go on vacation and have it still work.
Consultant: What would count as a win for whoever's above this?
Yvette Carnahan: Pete would count keeping Brightmoor as a win, and he'd count not hiring a tenth person into client services as a win. Hollis would count the county contract as a win.
Consultant: Hollis is?
Yvette Carnahan: The owner. He's not in the weeds on this. He'll ask Pete whether it's a good idea, and Pete will ask me.
Consultant: So walk me through the decision. If you and I agree what to do, what actually happens?

Yvette Carnahan: I decide the tool. That's mine, client services is my department and this is my problem. The money is Pete's. Anything over ten thousand he signs off, and over fifty he'd want Hollis to nod at it.
Consultant: Has he bought software before?
Yvette Carnahan: He bought monday, two years ago. [laughs] So.
Curtis Vandergrift: He bought monday because I asked him for it, and then it didn't get used, and he has mentioned that to me more than once since.
Consultant: That's honest, thank you. So what does Pete need to see this time?
Yvette Carnahan: He needs to see that somebody other than Curtis is going to keep it alive. And he needs to see what it costs next to what it saves, and he'll want that second part in writing.
Consultant: Would he come to a working session?
Yvette Carnahan: If I tell him it's about the January renewal, he'll come.
Consultant: Good. On timing, is this a this-quarter thing or a next-year thing?
Yvette Carnahan: It's a before-December thing. I want to put something in front of Brightmoor at the December quarterly, even if it's partial. Then January is the renewal decision.
Consultant: And what could get in the way of this going ahead at all?
Yvette Carnahan: Pete. Not because he's difficult, because he's careful. And the memory of the last one.

Curtis Vandergrift: And me, a bit. I'm one person. I've got the phones, the laptops, Sage, the network, and now this. If it's built so that every little change is a ticket to me, it'll die the same way it died last time.
Consultant: That's a good thing to say out loud. Would you want to be the person who can change it?
Curtis Vandergrift: I want to be able to add a column without calling a consultant. No offence.
Consultant: None taken. That's how it should end up.

Tansy Whitlock: Can I say the other risk? My team. Not because they won't like it. Because if it's slower than the spreadsheet on a Tuesday at nine with four phones going, they'll go back to the spreadsheet and I won't be able to stop them.
Consultant: That's the most useful thing anyone's said to me about adoption. What would make it faster than the spreadsheet?
Tansy Whitlock: Not typing the client and the building and the contact every single time. None of those change.

Consultant: Noted, and that's a fair test. Now, there are some things you've each said you want, and I want to be straight with you about the order they can happen in. Curtis, you mentioned single sign-on earlier.
Curtis Vandergrift: Yeah. I'd want Microsoft sign-in. We're all Microsoft 365. I don't want another password for ninety field guys, and half of them haven't got a company email address anyway.

Consultant: Those are two separate problems, and I'll come back to both, because what's available depends on which plan you're really on, and neither of us knows that yet. That's one of the things I'd check first.
Curtis Vandergrift: Fair.

Yvette Carnahan: The one I really want is a portal. Where Brightmoor's property managers log in and see their own work orders and their own response times, so we're not sat there arguing about whose spreadsheet is right.

Consultant: I understand why, and I want to be honest about the sequence. A client-facing portal, turning an email into a work order automatically, and setting up service-level policies that work the clock out per contract, those are all real things and they're all a later phase. What I'd rather do first is get every work order into one place with an owner, a priority and a target date, and get the report coming out of the system. Then those three go on a list for after that.
Yvette Carnahan: How much later?
Consultant: I'll be specific about that once we've agreed the first piece, and I'd rather under-promise it than have you tell Pete something I then have to walk back.
Yvette Carnahan: Okay. But the email one is the one that bit us in July. If it can't read the inbox, what stops the Friday afternoon chiller happening again?

Consultant: On day one somebody still opens the inbox. What changes is that when they do, it goes into a queue with a clock on it instead of staying an email. The queue is what makes it visible and the clock is what makes it loud, including on a Saturday. Reading the inbox automatically makes that better later, but it isn't the thing that makes it work.
Yvette Carnahan: All right. I can live with that.
Tansy Whitlock: Honestly, if it just stopped being an inbox I'd take that today.

Consultant: And on the service levels, for the first version I'd carry the window as a priority and a target date on each work order, in your words, so emergency, urgent, routine, and you can see what's about to breach. Working it out from each contract automatically is part of that later phase.
Yvette Carnahan: As long as I can see what's late. That's what I need in December.
Consultant: Understood. One thing I'd want before I design the escalation part: I'd like to talk to a supervisor.
Yvette Carnahan: Talk to Dewey. And don't design it for a desk. He'll look at it on a phone in a parking lot, or he won't look at it at all.
Consultant: That's exactly why I want to talk to him first.
Curtis Vandergrift: Can I ask something? I could probably put most of this together myself, honestly. What am I buying if you do it?
Consultant: You could, you've done it once. The questions I'd ask you are what held it up last time, and whose week it comes out of this time.
Curtis Vandergrift: [laughs] Yeah. Nobody asked the help desk, and it came out of a Saturday.

Consultant: Then you've answered it better than I would have. I'd rather you spent your time on the part only you can do, which is the Microsoft side and the access, and have the shape of the thing come out of a conversation with Tansy's people.
Curtis Vandergrift: That's reasonable.

Yvette Carnahan: Two things from me. One, we had a demo in the spring from a proper facilities system. Full [inaudible], asset registers, PM schedules, mobile app for the technicians, the lot. It was a lot of money, it was a six-month implementation, and we'd have had to move things out of Sage into it. I didn't hate it. I just can't do it this year.
Consultant: What would make the choice between the two clear for you?
Yvette Carnahan: Whether I can get to December with something that works. If the answer is no, I may as well do the big thing properly next year and take my chances with Brightmoor.
Consultant: That's the right test, and I'll answer it straight rather than optimistically when I've put the plan together.
Yvette Carnahan: Two. Can you send me something with a number on it? Pete is going to ask what it costs before he gives me twenty minutes of his day.

Consultant: I'd rather not put a number in front of Pete before you and I have agreed what's in the first piece, because then the number means something. What I'll send you is a short recap of what I heard today in plain language, and the shape of what I'd propose. Then we agree the scope with you and Pete in the room, and the number comes with that.
Yvette Carnahan: Fine. I've been on the other end of that conversation, so, fine.

Consultant: Let me play back what I think the first piece is, and tell me where I've got it wrong. One, every work order in one queue however it arrives, with the client, the building, a priority in your language, an owner and a target date.

Consultant: Two, escalation to the right supervisor as something you can see the state of, designed for a phone. Three, the monthly report coming out of the system per client, with the PM completion part still coming from Delia and Sage for now.
Consultant: Four, the two clients' own portals stay manual for now, and we look later at whether any of that can come down. Is that the first cut?
